videos.title: How a Circle works
videos.description: A short introduction to reading, respectful disagreement and sharing with care. Original silent SoE video with captions.
videos.credit: Original Society of Explorers text and canvas graphics. No third-party media, audio, music or voice.
videos.transcript:
How a Circle works
Read. Reflect. Share.
A good conversation starts with a good question.

Choose a Circle
Find a time and place that work for you.
Read the source before your meeting.

Bring your perspective
Christian and conservative roots.
Every faith and view is welcome.

Make room for disagreement
Challenge an idea.
Treat the person with respect.

Share with care
Keep other members’ words private.
Ask before recording.

Start with the reading
Find a Circle. Read.
Join the conversation.

videos.title: Who gets the night sky?
videos.description: The Archivist looks at actual 2026 footage from Paranal, Chile, and asks how we should weigh satellite internet against a shared night sky. A silent 24-second Reel.

attribution.edits: Trimmed, framed vertically and annotated with AI-assisted commentary. Source audio omitted.

videos.transcript:
The night sky has traffic. A time-lapse
excerpt from Paranal, Chile, filmed May 19,
2026.

A lifeline far from a tower. Satellite
internet can connect places beyond ground
networks.

A cost for the telescope. Bright trails can
obscure part of a telescope image.

Who gets the night sky? What brightness
limit would you set? Bring your reason to a
Circle.

videos.title: What did the tilt prove?
videos.description: The Archivist uses actual footage of the October 2026 telescope tilt test in Chile to ask what one successful test proves. A silent 20-second Reel.

attribution.edits: Trimmed, framed vertically and annotated with AI-assisted commentary. Source audio omitted.

videos.transcript:
Almost 2,000 tonnes tilt. The frame of ESO’s
new telescope tilted in October.

The trick? A film of oil. About 120 microns
thick in this test, says ESO.

What did it prove? The frame can tilt on one
axis. Sharp images take another test.

What would convince you? Which test would
you ask for? Bring your reason to a Circle.

videos.title: Which height are we measuring?
videos.description: The Archivist uses archive footage of Kīlauea to explain two measurements from the October 17, 2026 eruption. A silent 20-second Reel.

attribution.edits: Trimmed and framed with original, AI-assisted educational commentary. Archive footage is labeled throughout.

videos.transcript:
Archive footage of Kīlauea. 25,000 feet?
What went up? USGS reported two heights for
the eruption on October 17, 2026.

The plume rose to about 25,000 feet above
sea level.

The lava fountain at the north vent peaked
at just over 700 feet by 5 a.m. local time.

Ask what they measured. Which feature? Where
did they measure from? Bring a question to a
Circle.
